hook.text: Jakob Fugger was the richest person in history, adjusted for inflation. His bank financed kings, emperors, and popes.

buildup.text: The Fugger bank lent Charles V the money to buy his election as Holy Roman Emperor in 1519. Literally bought a crown.

discovery.text: In return, the Fuggers got mining monopolies across Europe. Their bank controlled silver and copper markets for decades.

twist.text: When kings couldn't repay, the Fuggers lost everything. Spain's defaults wiped out the family's banking empire.

climax.text: The Fuggers learned the oldest banking lesson: lending to kings is profitable until the king decides not to pay.

punchline.text: Lend to a king. Get rich. Then watch the king not pay you back.

quiz.question: What destroyed the Fugger banking empire?

details.summary: The Fugger family of Augsburg became the richest bankers in 16th-century Europe by financing emperors, popes, and kings. At their peak, the Fuggers were wealthier than the Medici and had more power than many monarchs who borrowed from them.
details.whyItMatters: The Fugger dynasty demonstrated that banking power could surpass royal authority. Their ability to finance wars and elections showed how financial capital could become the ultimate political weapon.
takeaways: Jakob Fugger financed the election of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V
The Fugger fortune at its peak would exceed $400 billion in today's dollars
They charged interest to the Catholic Church while usury was officially banned

faq.question: How did the Fuggers become the richest family in Europe?
faq.answer: They started in the textile trade, expanded into silver and copper mining, then leveraged their wealth to become bankers to the Habsburgs. Lending to emperors brought monopoly mining rights and trade privileges that multiplied their fortune.

faq.question: What caused the Fugger banking empire to decline?
faq.answer: Overlending to the Spanish crown, which defaulted on its debts multiple times, gradually eroded Fugger capital. The family transitioned from banking to landed aristocracy, and their financial empire was eclipsed by Dutch and English banks.
